text:
Where was she going? Home—to her own home? Filippo would have taken her back. To Filippo’s house?
His mother would have died of it. And by that hour Filippo must already have read the few lines Loredana had left him: “I shall never forget thee; I shall always love thee; the farther away I seem to thee, the more shall I be thine....” And after this, would she have gone back to him, with bowed head, like a repentant schoolgirl, and still too late to be forgiven?

Once more she saw that accursed, half-naked woman with goat-like feet, who, with her right arm raised, seemed to command her to stop. She turned, and on the other side saw Berto, who dared not move to detain her, dared not speak lest he frighten her, and kept watching her, trying to divine from her gestures what decision she would make.

She returned to her armchair, let herself fall into it, and said not a word.

Thus followed an anguished silence of several minutes, during which Loredana and Berto stared keenly at one another, motionless, as though searching each other; but Berto could endure it no longer. He approached her again and seized her hands.

“Stay!” he said, his voice veiled by passion. “Stay! I beseech thee! I know thou dost not love me, and that does not frighten me....”

He was trying to remove one of her gloves; she noticed, and unbuttoned it with a quick gesture, offering him her bare hand and wrist to kiss; but when she felt those avid lips upon her flesh, she turned her head away as though in disgust.

“No!” she said. “Wait!”

She seized the goblet and drained it avidly, then held it out to Berto again so that he might pour more, and drank once more; but, catching sight of herself in the mirror, she flung the empty goblet to the floor, where it shattered.

“What do you wish to do with me?” she then said.

“Everything thou shalt command me to do,” Berto replied. “I am free; I can leave this very day, tonight, tomorrow, whenever thou askest it of me.”

“Yes,” Loredana declared. “We shall leave at once. We shall go to Rome.”

She burst into so harsh and sardonic a laugh that Berto looked at her in alarm.

“To Rome,” Loredana repeated. “I was to go there with Flopi; I shall go with you. Is it not the same? Am I not your mistress? Did they not want me to be your mistress? One man or another matters little.... Why do we not go to Sirmione as well?... I want to trample upon all my past, I want to destroy every memory, I want nothing to remain, nothing at all of what was so dear to me and would make me blush!... Ah, you do not know the horror I feel for life!... You think only of possessing me; I see it in your eyes, and you do not understand that I am no longer alive, you do not understand that I hate you, and the nearer you come to me, the more I hate you!...”

Berto did not answer, but the hand holding the young woman’s loosened its grip; he drew back, struck by the savage vehemence of those words.

“Why do you want me?” Loredana continued, casting him a contemptuous glance. “I love Filippo, and I sacrifice myself for him. Is that not clear? Is it not clear that I want to ruin myself in order to save him? Have I not told you already! And I chose you in particular so that he might despise me so much that he would seek me no more!... And you lend yourself to this game?... If I consented to become your mistress, that would be the moment when I loved Filippo most, because it would be the gravest sacrifice I could make for him.... And have you not understood? How must I tell you that I shall never love you?”

Cornered by that ferocious logic, which seemed dictated by the need to bite and destroy with which Loredana felt herself vibrating through and through, Berto at first found no answer; then he uttered the single phrase that explained any madness:

“But I love thee,” he said. “I love thee, Loredana; and I know nothing else....”

The young woman looked at him, sensing that he was not lying; he seemed submissive and defeated to her, and she pitied him.

“Come,” she murmured, rising, “let me go!”

“Where, where dost thou wish to go?” Berto asked, taking a step toward her. “Where dost thou wish to go, like this?”

She had started toward the door, without a hat, like a madwoman.

Berto looked at her, elegant and slender in her perfectly plain amethyst-colored dress, gracefully adorned with a strip of dark fur that ran around her breast and along the bottom hem of her skirt like a little serpent.

She was going out, departing, fleeing; suddenly she had felt that the sacrifice was too repugnant, that it was better to die, to rest, to think of no one ever again, and she had remembered the black, deep canal flowing before Berto’s house.

The hour was late, the light dim, the people few on that winter evening. Loredana could have thrown herself into the water and drowned there without anyone coming to her aid.

“Where dost thou wish to go?” Berto repeated.

They met upon the threshold and stared at one another, he with eyes blazing with desire, she with the lost gaze of despair; but when she tried to go on, he seized her by the arms and held her back.

Loredana broke into laughter once more.

In her mouth was the taste of that mud from which human beings drink, that mud which is all of life, and an unslaked burning scorched her veins, as though she had swallowed liquid fire....

Someone behind Berto—perhaps the half-naked woman with goat-like feet—suggested a thought to him: the young woman would never bring herself either to leave or to remain, either to live or to die; she had to be forced.

He drew her abruptly to his breast, sealed her mouth with his own, giving her so long a kiss that he seemed to wish to drink her life, her soul, her blood; he felt Loredana gradually yielding, bending backward, and he followed the movement without taking his mouth from the coveted mouth, and laid her upon the broad divan.




XVII.


It was a joyous spring, that of 1894 in Venice. An immense host of foreigners descended from every part of the world, women and men already drunk with delight and desire, their souls vibrating with that sensual romanticism inspired by languid Venice.

New passions and new dramas sprang up amid that throng of people, and on certain evenings Saint Mark’s Square became a wondrous drawing room through which the fashionable women of New York and Paris, London and Vienna, Berlin and Petersburg wandered, leaving in their wake a trail of exotic perfumes.

They saw Venice through the eyes of legend and history, and their souls were transformed, pouring themselves forth and becoming perverted among the treasures of art and the deathly silence of the voluptuous city. The gondola, slow and caressing, agile and silent, made them dream the erotic dreams and swift tragedies of novels; the night, whether illumined by moonlight upon the narrow waterways and canals, or dark, or veiled, seemed to them as enigmatic and extravagant as in no other city in the world.
